claims.text: Variations in alloy chemistry alter stacking-fault energy in equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets.
Stacking-fault energy tunes the balance between deformation twinning and dislocation glide.
The balance between deformation twinning and dislocation glide governs yield strength.
The balance between deformation twinning and dislocation glide governs ductility and failure mode.
The selected alloys can be prepared as homogenized, single-phase FCC microstructures using standardized thermomechanical treatments.
Elemental substitutions in this alloy family modify stacking-fault energy.
Lower stacking-fault energy promotes deformation-twin formation.
Higher stacking-fault energy favors dislocation glide.
Dislocation-glide-dominated deformation leads to localized deformation and may reduce toughness.
Alloys with lower predicted stacking-fault energy than the equiatomic quinary baseline will develop greater deformation-twin density.
Alloys with lower predicted stacking-fault energy than the baseline will exhibit higher strain-hardening rates.
Alloys with lower predicted stacking-fault energy than the baseline will exhibit improved ductility.
Alloys with higher stacking-fault energy than the baseline will display dislocation-slip-dominated deformation.
Alloys with higher stacking-fault energy than the baseline will have lower work-hardening capacity.
Alloys with higher stacking-fault energy than the baseline will have reduced toughness.
The proposed relationships are limited to single-phase FCC alloys processed under standardized conditions and deformed at room temperature.
Significant second-phase formation or predominant grain-boundary segregation may invalidate the proposed relationship.
